authored_against: Grade 7 science, middle band. Keys state established science at this grade band; they are not extracted from the source, which states only a focus and generic objectives.

fixed_facts: Atoms are the particles that make up elements; molecules are groups of atoms bonded together.
relationships: All matter is made of atoms, and atoms of a given element are alike in the properties that define that element.
A molecule is two or more atoms held together by chemical bonds; a compound contains atoms of more than one element in a fixed ratio.
Substances differ because their atoms differ, or because the same atoms are arranged and bonded differently.
accepted_alternative_framings: Ball-and-stick, space-filling, and symbolic formula representations are all valid molecular models; the choice is judged on what it needs to show.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming atoms of a compound take on the bulk properties of the compound, such as a single water molecule being wet.
Claiming a compound is a mixture of its elements that keeps their properties.
Claiming atoms can be seen directly with a school microscope.
topics.out_of_scope: Subatomic structure in detail, electron configuration, and bonding theory are Grade 8 and High School work.

fixed_facts: A pure substance has a fixed composition; a mixture does not.
relationships: A pure substance, whether an element or a compound, has a fixed composition and a characteristic set of properties.
A mixture contains two or more substances in no fixed ratio, and each keeps its own properties.
Mixtures are separated by physical means; the components of a compound are separated only by chemical change.
accepted_alternative_framings: Homogeneous and heterogeneous, or uniform and non-uniform, are both acceptable ways to sort mixtures.
disqualifying_errors: Classifying a compound as a mixture because it contains more than one element.
Claiming a solution is a pure substance because it looks uniform.
Claiming a mixture has a fixed composition.
topics.out_of_scope: Chromatographic and distillation theory, and phase diagrams, are High School work.

relationships: A physical property can be observed without changing the substance into a different substance; a chemical property describes how it changes into one.
Characteristic properties such as melting point, boiling point, density, and solubility do not depend on how much of the substance there is, so they can identify it.
Identification is stronger when several characteristic properties agree.
accepted_alternative_framings: Intensive and extensive, or characteristic and non-characteristic, are both acceptable ways to make the amount-independence distinction.
disqualifying_errors: Treating mass or volume as a property that identifies a substance.
Claiming flammability or reactivity can be observed without any change occurring.
Identifying a substance from a single property and stating it as certain.
topics.out_of_scope: Quantitative density calculation is acceptable but not required; spectroscopic identification is High School work.

relationships: Synthetic materials are made by processing natural resources so that new substances with new properties are produced.
The properties of a synthetic material come from its composition and structure, which is why they can be designed for a purpose.
Every synthetic material carries costs as well as benefits, in resources used, energy required, and what happens at the end of its life.
accepted_alternative_framings: Plastics, alloys, synthetic fibres, and engineered ceramics are all correct examples.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming synthetic materials are not made from natural resources.
Claiming synthetic means harmful and natural means safe.
Claiming a material's properties can be chosen independently of its structure.
topics.out_of_scope: Polymerisation chemistry and materials-science structure-property theory are High School work.

relationships: Every model of matter simplifies, and the simplification determines what the model can and cannot explain.
A model is chosen for the question being asked; a model that is wrong for one purpose can be right for another.
Stating a model's limitation is part of using it correctly, not an admission of failure.
disqualifying_errors: Treating a model's simplification as a property of the real system, such as claiming atoms are coloured spheres.
Claiming a more detailed model is always the better one.
Using a model outside the range it was built for without saying so.
topics.out_of_scope: Formal model validation and computational modelling are later work.

relationships: Measured properties are the evidence for a claim about what a substance is.
The strength of the evidence depends on how characteristic the property is and how well it was measured.
A property measurement that disagrees with the identification is reported and explained, not dropped.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming an identification is confirmed while omitting a measurement that disagrees.
Using a non-characteristic property, such as mass, as identification evidence.
Reporting a property measurement with no unit or no method.
topics.out_of_scope: Uncertainty propagation and statistical comparison to reference values are High School work.

relationships: A chemical reaction produces one or more substances with properties different from the starting substances.
Signs that suggest a reaction include gas production, a temperature change not caused by external heating or cooling, a colour change, a precipitate, light, and a new odour.
Each sign has non-chemical explanations too, so a conclusion rests on several lines of evidence together.
disqualifying_errors: Treating bubbling alone as proof of reaction when boiling or escaping dissolved gas explains it.
Claiming any colour change establishes a chemical reaction.
Claiming dissolving is always a chemical reaction.
topics.out_of_scope: Reaction classification, equilibrium, and mechanism are High School work.

fixed_facts: Reactants are the starting substances; products are the substances formed.
relationships: Reactants are the substances present before a reaction; products are the substances present after it.
The atoms in the products are the same atoms that were in the reactants, rearranged into new combinations.
The products have their own properties, which is what distinguishes a reaction from a mixture.
accepted_alternative_framings: Word equations and formula equations are both acceptable representations at this grade.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming new atoms are made during a chemical reaction.
Claiming the products retain the properties of the reactants.
Writing products on the reactant side of a representation, or the reverse.
topics.out_of_scope: Balancing equations quantitatively, the mole, and limiting reactants are High School work.

fixed_facts: The number of atoms of each element is the same before and after a chemical reaction, so the total mass is unchanged.
relationships: Atoms are neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction; they are rearranged.
Because the atoms are conserved, the total mass of the system is the same before and after.
An apparent mass change in an open container means matter crossed the boundary, most often as a gas.
accepted_alternative_framings: Conservation of mass and conservation of atoms are two statements of the same principle at this grade.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming mass is lost when a substance burns, without accounting for gases released or oxygen consumed.
Claiming atoms of one element convert into another element in a chemical reaction.
Concluding conservation of mass fails from an open-system measurement.
topics.out_of_scope: Nuclear reactions, where element identity does change, and mass-energy equivalence are High School work.

fixed_facts: An exothermic process releases energy to its surroundings; an endothermic process absorbs energy from them.
relationships: Some reactions release energy to the surroundings and some absorb energy from them.
A container that becomes warmer indicates energy released by the reaction inside it; one that becomes cooler indicates energy absorbed.
Energy released or absorbed is transferred, not created or destroyed.
accepted_alternative_framings: Describing a reaction as exothermic, or as releasing energy or giving out heat, are all correct.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming an endothermic reaction creates cold rather than absorbing energy.
Claiming a reaction generates energy from nothing.
Reading the container's temperature change as the reaction's own temperature without saying what was measured.
topics.out_of_scope: Bond energies, enthalpy, and calorimetric calculation are High School work.

relationships: Evidence that a reaction occurred is a measured or observed change in properties, recorded before and after under the same conditions.
A control, in which the suspected cause is absent, distinguishes the reaction from something else in the setup.
The strength of the conclusion depends on how many independent signs point the same way.
disqualifying_errors: Concluding a reaction occurred from one ambiguous sign with no control.
Reporting only the observations that support the expected conclusion.
Comparing before and after under different conditions and attributing the difference to reaction.
topics.out_of_scope: Analytical confirmation methods and quantitative yield are High School work.

relationships: A device that releases or absorbs thermal energy works by controlling the rate of transfer between a source and its surroundings.
Insulating materials slow transfer; they do not produce warmth or cold.
The device is judged against measurable criteria, such as how far the temperature changed and how long the effect lasted.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming an insulator generates warmth or cold.
Claiming a device creates thermal energy rather than releasing or transferring it.
Declaring a design successful without measuring against the stated criteria.
topics.out_of_scope: Thermal conductivity values, heat-transfer coefficients, and efficiency calculation are High School work.

fixed_facts: Temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of the particles in a sample.
relationships: The particles in any sample of matter are in constant motion, and temperature measures the average kinetic energy of that motion.
Temperature and total thermal energy are different: a large cool object can contain more thermal energy than a small hot one.
Adding energy to a sample generally raises its temperature, except during a change of state, when it changes the arrangement of particles instead.
accepted_alternative_framings: Describing temperature as average particle motion or as average kinetic energy per particle are both correct.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming temperature and thermal energy are the same quantity.
Claiming particles stop moving at ordinary cold temperatures.
Claiming temperature rises steadily while a substance is melting or boiling.
topics.out_of_scope: Absolute zero, the kinetic theory in quantitative form, and specific heat calculations are High School work.

fixed_facts: Conduction transfers energy through direct particle contact, convection through the bulk movement of a fluid, and radiation by electromagnetic waves requiring no medium.
relationships: Conduction transfers energy through collisions between neighbouring particles, so it needs matter in contact.
Convection transfers energy by the bulk movement of a heated fluid, so it happens in liquids and gases, not in solids.
Radiation transfers energy as electromagnetic waves and is the only mechanism that works across a vacuum.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming convection occurs within a solid.
Claiming radiation requires a medium to travel through.
Claiming energy from the Sun reaches Earth mainly by conduction or convection.
topics.out_of_scope: Quantitative transfer equations and emissivity are High School work.

fixed_facts: Thermal energy is transferred spontaneously from the higher-temperature object to the lower-temperature one.
relationships: When objects at different temperatures interact, energy is transferred from the warmer to the cooler until they reach the same temperature.
The transfer is one-directional on its own; energy does not move spontaneously from cooler to warmer.
Total energy is conserved during the transfer: what one object loses, the other and the surroundings gain.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming cold flows from the cooler object into the warmer one.
Claiming energy is lost rather than transferred to the surroundings.
Claiming a warmer object can spontaneously take energy from a cooler one.
topics.out_of_scope: The second law stated formally, entropy, and refrigeration cycles are High School work.

relationships: For the same energy input, a larger mass of the same material changes temperature less than a smaller mass.
Different materials require different amounts of energy to change the temperature of the same mass by the same amount.
Comparing materials fairly requires the same mass, the same energy input, and the same starting temperature.
accepted_alternative_framings: Naming this property specific heat capacity is correct but not required at this grade.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming equal energy input produces equal temperature change regardless of mass.
Claiming all materials respond identically to the same energy input.
Comparing materials tested at different masses or starting temperatures without saying so.
topics.out_of_scope: The specific heat equation and calorimetry calculations are High School work.

fixed_facts: Kinetic energy is energy of motion; potential energy is energy stored by position or configuration.
relationships: Kinetic energy depends on an object's mass and speed; potential energy depends on position or arrangement relative to something else.
Energy converts between kinetic and potential forms while the total stays the same, apart from what is transferred out of the system.
Potential energy is a property of a system, such as an object and Earth together, not of the object alone.
accepted_alternative_framings: Gravitational, elastic, and chemical potential energy are all correct examples of stored energy.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming energy is destroyed when a moving object comes to rest, rather than transferred out.
Claiming potential energy belongs to the object by itself with no reference position or system.
Claiming kinetic energy depends only on speed, with mass making no difference.
topics.out_of_scope: Energy equations, and kinetic energy going with the square of speed, are High School work; a learner who uses them correctly is not wrong.

fixed_facts: No device converts all of its energy input into the useful output.
relationships: A device's useful output is always less than its energy input, because some energy is transferred to the surroundings, usually as warming.
Improving efficiency means reducing the unwanted transfers, not eliminating them.
Efficiency claims are judged against measurements of input and useful output, not against the design intent.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming a device is or could be one hundred per cent efficient.
Claiming a device produces more energy than it receives.
Reporting an efficiency without saying what was measured as input and as useful output.
topics.out_of_scope: Efficiency as a calculated percentage is acceptable but not required; the second law and Carnot limits are High School work.

fixed_facts: All living things are made of one or more cells, the cell is the basic unit of structure and function, and all cells come from pre-existing cells.
relationships: All living organisms are composed of one or more cells.
The cell is the basic unit of structure and function in living things.
All cells arise from pre-existing cells; cells do not form spontaneously from non-living material.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming some living organisms are not made of cells.
Claiming cells form spontaneously from non-living matter.
Claiming viruses are cells.
topics.out_of_scope: Cell-cycle detail, prokaryote-eukaryote molecular differences, and endosymbiosis are High School work.

fixed_facts: The nucleus contains the cell's genetic material; the cell membrane controls what enters and leaves; chloroplasts are found in plant cells and not in animal cells.
relationships: Each cell part carries out a particular function, and the parts work together as a system.
The cell membrane controls what enters and leaves the cell; the nucleus holds the genetic material in cells that have one.
Plant cells have a cell wall and chloroplasts that animal cells lack; both have a membrane, cytoplasm, and, in eukaryotes, a nucleus.
accepted_alternative_framings: Naming a structure's function in everyday terms is acceptable, provided the function is right.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming animal cells contain chloroplasts or a cell wall.
Claiming the cell wall, rather than the membrane, controls what enters and leaves a plant cell.
Claiming every cell has a nucleus; bacterial cells do not.
topics.out_of_scope: Organelle biochemistry, membrane transport mechanisms, and the endomembrane system are High School work.

relationships: A unicellular organism carries out all life functions within a single cell.
In a multicellular organism, cells are specialised, and groups of them carry out different functions for the whole organism.
Being unicellular is not a lesser condition; unicellular organisms are complete, successful organisms.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming unicellular organisms cannot carry out all the functions of life.
Claiming a colony of identical cells is the same as a multicellular organism with specialised cells.
Claiming multicellular organisms are more advanced in a way that makes unicellular ones incomplete.
topics.out_of_scope: Differentiation mechanisms and stem-cell biology are High School work.

fixed_facts: The levels of organisation run cells, tissues, organs, organ systems, organism.
relationships: Similar specialised cells form tissues, tissues form organs, organs form organ systems, and systems together form the organism.
Each level does something the level below cannot do on its own; the organisation is what produces the capability.
A failure at one level affects the levels above it.
disqualifying_errors: Placing the levels of organisation out of order.
Claiming an organ is made of a single kind of cell.
Claiming organ systems operate independently of one another.
topics.out_of_scope: Histology and developmental biology are High School work.

relationships: A microscope image is a two-dimensional view of a thin slice or a thin sample, so what is seen depends on how the sample was prepared.
Magnification and the scale bar are needed before any size can be read from an image.
Stains and preparation can introduce features that are artefacts rather than parts of the living cell.
disqualifying_errors: Reading a size off a micrograph with no scale or magnification given.
Claiming a structure is absent because it was not visible in one preparation.
Treating a preparation artefact as a cell structure.
topics.out_of_scope: Resolution limits, electron microscopy, and staining chemistry are High School work.

relationships: A cell's shape and contents relate to what it does, which is why nerve, muscle, and root-hair cells look so different.
Specialisation trades generality for capability: a specialised cell does one job well and depends on others for the rest.
Inferring function from structure is a hypothesis that must then be checked against evidence.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming a cell developed a structure because the organism needed it.
Asserting a function from appearance alone with no supporting evidence.
Claiming specialised cells can carry out every function independently.
topics.out_of_scope: Gene regulation of differentiation is High School work.

relationships: Body systems interact: the digestive, circulatory, respiratory, excretory, nervous, and musculoskeletal systems each depend on the others.
A substance taken in by one system is distributed by another and used or removed by a third.
Because the systems are coupled, a change in one produces changes in others.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming each body system works independently.
Tracing a substance through the body while skipping the system that actually transports it.
Claiming an effect on one system leaves the others unchanged.
topics.out_of_scope: Organ physiology in detail and quantitative modelling are High School work.

fixed_facts: Nerve cells carry information as electrical and chemical signals.
relationships: Sensory receptors detect a stimulus and send signals along nerve cells toward the brain and spinal cord.
Signals are processed in the brain or spinal cord, and signals are then sent out to muscles or glands to produce a response.
Signalling is fast compared with chemical messengers carried in the blood, which is why the nervous system handles rapid responses.
accepted_alternative_framings: Describing the pathway as receptor, processing, response, or as stimulus, integration, effector, are both correct.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming nerve signals travel as a fluid pushed along the nerve.
Claiming a response occurs without any processing anywhere.
Reversing the direction, with signals travelling from muscles to receptors as the normal pathway.
topics.out_of_scope: Action potentials, synaptic transmission, and neurotransmitters are High School work.

relationships: Each type of sensory receptor responds to a particular kind of stimulus, such as light, sound, pressure, temperature, or chemicals.
An organism can only respond to stimuli it has receptors for, which is why different animals sense different things.
Receptors convert the stimulus into a signal the nervous system can carry; they do not send the stimulus itself.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming one receptor type responds equally to every stimulus.
Claiming an organism senses something it has no receptor for.
Claiming the receptor sends the light or sound itself along the nerve.
topics.out_of_scope: Transduction mechanisms and receptor molecular biology are High School work.

relationships: A response follows a stimulus through a pathway of detection, processing, and action.
The same stimulus can produce different responses in different circumstances, because processing takes context into account.
Some responses are immediate and involuntary; others involve deliberate processing and take longer.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming every response to a stimulus is identical regardless of context.
Describing a response with no stimulus identified.
Claiming involuntary responses involve no signalling at all.
topics.out_of_scope: Reflex arc anatomy and conditioning theory are later work.

fixed_facts: Homeostasis is the maintenance of internal conditions within a range, not at a single fixed value.
relationships: Organisms maintain internal conditions such as temperature, water balance, and blood sugar within a workable range.
Maintenance requires detecting a departure from the range and acting to reverse it, which is a feedback process.
Internal conditions fluctuate within the range; homeostasis is regulation, not constancy.
accepted_alternative_framings: Describing the mechanism as negative feedback is correct, and describing it in plain terms as detecting and correcting is equally correct here.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming internal conditions are held perfectly constant.
Claiming homeostasis happens without any detection of the change.
Claiming a departure from the range is corrected by a process that pushes it further in the same direction.
topics.out_of_scope: Endocrine signalling detail and quantitative feedback modelling are High School work.

relationships: A model of coordination shows the systems involved, what passes between them, and in which direction.
The model has to include the detection step and the response step, or it cannot explain regulation.
A model is judged on whether it explains the coordination, not on how many parts it includes.
accepted_alternative_framings: Flow diagrams, labelled body diagrams, and written sequences are all valid model forms.
disqualifying_errors: Building a coordination model with no feedback path from response back to condition.
Showing systems connected with no statement of what passes between them.
Claiming the model represents the body completely.
topics.out_of_scope: Computational physiological modelling is later work.

relationships: The number of organisms an ecosystem supports is limited by the resources available: food, water, space, shelter, light, and nutrients.
When a resource becomes scarce, populations that depend on it decline or move.
The limiting resource is the one in shortest supply relative to need, and increasing any other does not remove the limit.
accepted_alternative_framings: Naming the idea a limiting factor is correct but not required at this grade.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming a population can grow indefinitely if food alone is plentiful.
Claiming resources are unlimited in a large ecosystem.
Claiming increasing a non-limiting resource increases the population.
topics.out_of_scope: Logistic growth equations and quantitative carrying capacity are High School work.

relationships: Competition occurs when organisms use the same limited resource, whether they are of the same species or different ones.
Predation transfers matter and energy from prey to predator and affects the population sizes of both.
Predator and prey populations influence each other, so a change in one produces a change in the other, usually after a delay.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming competition only occurs between different species.
Claiming predators eliminate their prey populations entirely as the normal outcome.
Claiming predator and prey populations change simultaneously with no delay.
topics.out_of_scope: Lotka-Volterra models and competitive exclusion by name are High School work.

fixed_facts: In mutualism both species benefit; in commensalism one benefits and the other is largely unaffected; in parasitism one benefits at the other's expense.
relationships: In a mutualistic relationship both species gain something, such as food, protection, or transport.
Mutualism is not cooperation by intention; each species is acting in ways that happen to benefit the other.
Mutualism, commensalism, and parasitism are distinguished by who benefits and who is harmed.
accepted_alternative_framings: Pollination, gut microbes, and lichen partnerships are all correct examples.
disqualifying_errors: Classifying a relationship as mutualism when only one species benefits.
Claiming the species involved intend to help each other.
Claiming parasitism always kills the host.
topics.out_of_scope: Coevolution and symbiosis theory in depth are High School work.

relationships: A food web shows feeding relationships, with arrows running from the organism that is eaten to the organism that eats it.
Because organisms appear in several chains, a change to one population can affect populations several links away.
Producers form the base of every web, and decomposers act on organisms at every level.
disqualifying_errors: Drawing food-web arrows from predator to prey.
Claiming the effect of removing a species is confined to its direct neighbours in the web.
Omitting producers or decomposers and calling the web complete.
topics.out_of_scope: Quantitative network analysis and trophic cascade modelling are High School work.

fixed_facts: Matter cycles within an ecosystem; energy flows through it and is not recycled.
relationships: Energy enters most ecosystems as sunlight, is captured by producers, and passes to consumers, with most released to the surroundings at each transfer.
Matter cycles: atoms pass between organisms and the environment repeatedly and are not used up.
Because most energy is lost at each transfer, ecosystems support far less biomass at higher feeding levels.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming energy cycles through an ecosystem the way matter does.
Claiming all the energy at one feeding level passes to the next.
Claiming matter is destroyed when an organism dies.
topics.out_of_scope: Specific trophic efficiency percentages and quantitative energy pyramids are High School work.

relationships: Ecosystems change over time through natural processes and through disturbance such as fire, flood, disease, and human activity.
After a disturbance, the community that returns may differ from the one before it.
An ecosystem's ability to recover depends on the severity of the disturbance and on what survives it.
accepted_alternative_framings: Naming the process succession is correct but not required at this grade.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming an undisturbed ecosystem stays permanently unchanged.
Claiming an ecosystem always returns to exactly its previous state after disturbance.
Claiming all disturbance is damaging; some species and communities depend on it.
topics.out_of_scope: Resilience metrics and succession modelling are High School work.

topics.focus: water cycle driven by energy and gravity
fixed_facts: The water cycle is driven by energy from the Sun and by gravity.
relationships: Energy from the Sun drives evaporation and transpiration, moving water from surface to atmosphere.
Gravity drives precipitation, runoff, and the downward movement of water through the ground.
Water changes state during the cycle but the total amount of water on Earth stays essentially the same.
accepted_alternative_framings: Including transpiration, sublimation, and infiltration among the processes is correct; naming every process is not required.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming the water cycle creates or destroys water.
Claiming clouds form because water becomes lighter than air rather than by condensation on particles.
Claiming the cycle runs without any energy input.
topics.out_of_scope: Quantitative water budgets and residence times are High School work.

fixed_facts: Weather changes occur at the boundaries between air masses of different temperature and humidity.
relationships: An air mass takes on the temperature and humidity of the region it forms over.
Where air masses of different properties meet, the warmer, less dense air is forced upward, it cools, water vapour condenses, and clouds and precipitation form.
The kind of weather depends on the properties of the air masses involved and on how they meet.
accepted_alternative_framings: Warm front, cold front, and occluded front are correct terms; a plain description of the interaction is equally acceptable.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming warm air sinks below cold air.
Claiming precipitation forms without air rising and cooling.
Claiming an air mass has the same properties wherever it forms.
topics.out_of_scope: Synoptic meteorology, adiabatic lapse rates, and numerical forecasting are High School work.

fixed_facts: Global circulation exists because the equator receives more solar energy per unit area than the poles.
relationships: Uneven heating of Earth's surface, with more energy per unit area near the equator, drives large-scale circulation in the atmosphere and ocean.
Circulation moves energy from lower to higher latitudes, which is why the poles are not colder and the tropics not hotter than they are.
Ocean currents and prevailing winds strongly influence the climate of the coasts they reach.
accepted_alternative_framings: Describing the cause as uneven heating, or as the angle at which sunlight strikes the surface, are both correct.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming the equator is warmer because it is closer to the Sun.
Claiming ocean currents have no effect on coastal climate.
Claiming circulation moves air and water without transporting energy.
topics.out_of_scope: Coriolis dynamics, Hadley cell mathematics, and thermohaline modelling are High School work.

relationships: A region's climate depends on latitude, elevation, distance from large water bodies, ocean currents, prevailing winds, and nearby mountains.
Two regions at the same latitude can have very different climates because of these other factors.
Climate is described by long-term averages and ranges, over decades rather than seasons.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming latitude alone determines climate.
Using a single season's weather to characterise a climate.
Claiming elevation has no effect on temperature.
topics.out_of_scope: Köppen classification and climate reanalysis data are High School work.

relationships: Weather maps show measured conditions and analysed features such as fronts, pressure centres, and precipitation, each with its own symbol.
A map is a snapshot with a stated time; reading a forecast from it requires knowing how the features move.
Air moves from higher pressure toward lower pressure, which is why pressure patterns indicate wind.
disqualifying_errors: Reading a weather map with no time stamp as showing current conditions.
Claiming air moves from low pressure toward high pressure.
Treating a map symbol as a measurement rather than as an analysed feature.
topics.out_of_scope: Isobar spacing and geostrophic wind calculation are High School work.

relationships: Weather and climate models are simplifications, so their predictions carry uncertainty that grows with the length of the forecast.
Uncertainty in a forecast is a statement about the model and the data, not an admission that the science is unreliable.
A forecast is evaluated over many predictions, not by whether one turned out right.
disqualifying_errors: Judging a probabilistic forecast wrong because a single day differed from it.
Claiming uncertainty means the model carries no information.
Presenting a model prediction as a measurement.
topics.out_of_scope: Ensemble forecasting and formal skill scores are High School work.

relationships: Natural hazards occur in patterns tied to geology, geography, and climate, so where they are likely can be mapped.
A hazard map shows likelihood and, usually, severity; it does not predict a particular event on a particular day.
Maps are built from historical records and physical understanding, and both have limits that belong in the reading.
disqualifying_errors: Reading a hazard map as a prediction of when an event will occur.
Claiming an area with no recorded event has no hazard.
Claiming hazards occur completely at random with no mappable pattern.
topics.out_of_scope: Return-period statistics and probabilistic hazard analysis are High School work.

relationships: Risk depends on the hazard, on what is exposed to it, and on how vulnerable that exposure is.
Two communities facing the same hazard can face very different risk, because exposure and vulnerability differ.
Reducing risk can act on exposure or on vulnerability, since the hazard itself cannot be prevented.
disqualifying_errors: Treating risk and hazard as the same thing.
Claiming equal hazard means equal risk regardless of who is exposed.
Claiming risk can be reduced to zero.
topics.out_of_scope: Quantitative risk assessment and insurance modelling are High School work.

relationships: Resources are distributed unevenly because of the geological and biological processes that formed them.
Extracting and using a resource changes the environment where it is taken and where it is used.
A renewable resource is only sustainable if the rate of use stays below the rate of replenishment.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming renewable resources cannot be depleted.
Claiming resource distribution is a matter of chance rather than of geological and biological process.
Claiming resource use can have no environmental effect.
topics.out_of_scope: Reserve estimation and resource economics are High School work.

relationships: Total impact depends on both the number of people and how much each consumes, so neither alone explains it.
Per-person consumption differs greatly between regions, so equal populations can have very different impacts.
Technology can change impact per person in either direction.
disqualifying_errors: Attributing environmental impact to population size alone.
Claiming per-person consumption is the same everywhere.
Claiming technological change always reduces impact.
topics.out_of_scope: Formal impact identities and demographic modelling are High School work.

fixed_facts: Global average surface temperature has risen since the late nineteenth century, and the increase in atmospheric carbon dioxide from burning fossil fuels is the principal cause.
relationships: Evidence for climate change comes from many independent lines: instrument records, ice cores, sea level, glacier extent, and the timing of biological events.
Independent lines of evidence agreeing is what makes the conclusion robust; no single record carries it alone.
Climate change is a change in long-term patterns, so it is established from decades of record, not from individual seasons.
accepted_alternative_framings: Describing the cause as greenhouse gases from human activity, or specifically as carbon dioxide from burning fossil fuels, are both correct.
disqualifying_errors: Citing one cold season as evidence against long-term warming.
Claiming the observed warming has no established cause.
Confusing the greenhouse effect, which is a natural and necessary process, with the enhanced effect caused by added greenhouse gases.
topics.out_of_scope: Radiative forcing calculations, climate sensitivity, and attribution methodology are High School work.

fixed_facts: Mitigation reduces the cause of a problem; adaptation reduces the harm from effects that occur anyway.
relationships: Mitigation acts on the cause, such as reducing emissions; adaptation acts on the consequences, such as changing where and how people build.
Both are needed, because some change is already committed and further change can still be limited.
Every option has costs, and who pays them and who benefits are part of the evaluation.
disqualifying_errors: Using mitigation and adaptation as though they meant the same thing.
Claiming adaptation removes the need to address the cause.
Presenting an option as having benefits with no costs.
topics.out_of_scope: Policy instruments and cost-benefit modelling are High School work.

relationships: A well-defined problem states criteria that can be measured and constraints that can be checked.
The definition comes before solution generation, so that all candidates are judged the same way.
Constraints include safety, cost, time, materials, and law, and none of them is traded away for performance.
disqualifying_errors: Writing a criterion that no test could evaluate.
Generating solutions before the problem is defined and then fitting criteria to the favourite.
Treating a safety constraint as negotiable.
topics.out_of_scope: Formal requirements engineering is later work.

relationships: Competing solutions are evaluated against the same criteria, using the same tests.
A solution can be better on one criterion and worse on another; the evaluation reports both rather than resolving it by preference.
A solution that fails a constraint is eliminated, not scored against the criteria.
accepted_alternative_framings: Systematic comparison by table or by written argument are both acceptable, provided the criteria are the same for each option.
disqualifying_errors: Comparing solutions tested under different conditions.
Declaring a winner without naming the criteria.
Retaining a solution that violates a stated constraint because it scores well elsewhere.
topics.out_of_scope: Weighted decision matrices with numeric weights are acceptable but not required; formal trade studies are later work.

relationships: Test data is only interpretable when the test conditions, the measured quantity, and the number of trials are recorded.
Repeated trials show whether a difference between designs is larger than the variation within a design.
A test that produced an unexpected result is reported as it happened.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming one design outperforms another from a difference smaller than the variation between trials.
Reporting test results without the conditions under which they were obtained.
Omitting a trial because its result was inconvenient.
topics.out_of_scope: Statistical significance testing is High School work.

relationships: A model is revised when its prediction and the test result disagree, and the revision names what the disagreement showed.
Changing one aspect at a time keeps the effect of each change identifiable.
A model that has never been tested against data has not yet been evaluated, however reasonable it looks.
disqualifying_errors: Revising a model to fit data without saying what the disagreement showed.
Changing several aspects at once and attributing the improvement to one.
Treating an untested model as validated.
topics.out_of_scope: Formal model calibration and parameter fitting are later work.

relationships: Optimising means improving performance against the criteria within the constraints, not improving everything at once.
Improving one criterion often worsens another, so optimisation involves choosing which trade-off to accept.
An optimum is relative to the criteria chosen; different criteria give a different optimum.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming a design was optimised on every criterion simultaneously.
Optimising past a constraint and reporting the result as a solution.
Presenting an optimum without stating the criteria it is optimal for.
topics.out_of_scope: Mathematical optimisation methods are later work.

relationships: Communicating a design decision means stating the criteria, the evidence, what was given up, and why.
A trade-off that is not stated has not been avoided; it has only been hidden from the reader.
The audience decides what detail is needed, but the evidence and its limits are always included.
disqualifying_errors: Presenting a chosen design as having no drawbacks.
Reporting a recommendation with no evidence behind it.
Omitting the limits of the testing from the communication.
topics.out_of_scope: Formal technical writing standards are later work.
